body.hook: What do you do when nobody tells you what to do? Maybe you cook, draw, fix bikes, edit videos or organize events. Those interests are clues. In CTF, you'll use them to explore the kinds of work that might fit you, by actually trying things, not just reading about them.

study.title: Interest Explorer
study.question: How can my interests point toward careers?
study.passage:
The five career clusters used in Alberta CTF:
1. Business, Finance and Information Technology (for example, entrepreneur, accountant, computer programmer)
2. Health, Recreation and Human Services (for example, nurse, chef, personal trainer, early childhood educator)
3. Media, Design and Communication Arts (for example, graphic designer, filmmaker, fashion designer)
4. Natural Resources (for example, agrologist, forestry technician, environmental scientist)
5. Trades, Manufacturing and Transportation (for example, electrician, carpenter, automotive technician, welder)
Part 1, Interest inventory (10 minutes): Rate 20 activity cards from 1 (not for me) to 5 (love it): cooking a meal, building a shelf, designing a logo, coding a game, caring for animals, fixing a bike, planning an event, filming a video and so on.
Part 2, Sort (10 minutes): Place your top-rated cards on a career-cluster chart. Which cluster has the most?
Part 3, Quick challenge (20 minutes): At stations, try a 5-minute mini-task from three clusters: design a logo (media), budget a class party (business), build a paper bridge that holds a textbook (trades).
Part 4, Reflect: Which task did you enjoy most? Which skills did you use?

body.objective: Students will be able to read a challenge brief and set criteria.

body.hook: A restaurant asks a team to invent a new lunch item. Without rules, one person makes soup, one makes cake, and one makes a sandwich nobody can afford. A clear brief with criteria keeps everyone working toward the same target.

study.title: Decode the Brief
study.question: How does a clear brief lead to clear criteria?
study.passage:
Sample brief (written for this lesson):
"The Grade 6 class is holding a reading celebration and needs a bookmark for each student. Each bookmark must be 5 cm by 20 cm, fit in a paperback, show the school's reading slogan and be made from materials already in our room. The class needs 30 bookmarks in two lessons, and the cost must stay under 10 dirhams in total."
Part 1: Highlight the client (who), the need (what), the constraints (limits) and any hints about what the client values.
Part 2: Turn the brief into four to six criteria. Good criteria are specific and measurable: "Bookmark is 5 cm by 20 cm (± 2 mm)" is better than "Bookmark is a good size."
Part 3: Swap criteria with a partner. Can each criterion be checked with a ruler, a count, a test or a simple yes/no? Rewrite any that cannot.

body.objective: Students will be able to make a plan with steps, materials and time.

successCriteria: I can break a challenge into steps
I can list the materials, tools and time I need

body.hook: A school bake sale opens in two hours, and the oven is still cold, nobody bought flour and three people are making the same cookies. Planning is the boring part that makes the exciting part work.

vocabulary.definition: A set of steps that shows how a challenge will be completed.

study.title: Plan It Out
study.question: How does a good plan make a challenge possible?
study.passage:
Challenge (written for this lesson): Your team has three 50-minute lessons to make a set of 30 reading-celebration bookmarks that meet your criteria from last lesson.
Planning template:
1. Steps: List every step in order, from "collect materials" to "deliver to the Grade 6 class."
2. Materials and tools: For each step, list what is used up (materials) and what is reused (tools).
3. Time: Estimate minutes for each step. Add the times. Do they fit in 150 minutes? If not, cut, combine or speed up steps.
4. Roles: Who does each step?
5. Milestones: Mark two checkpoints, for example "first bookmark finished and checked against criteria."
6. Contingency: Write one problem that might happen (for example, the laminator breaks) and what you will do.
